title: How to Win Friends and Influence People
author: Dale Carnegie

chapters.title: If You Want to Gather Honey, Don't Kick Over the Beehive
chapters.keys: Do not criticize, condemn or complain. When someone at work or at home gets something wrong, hold the cutting remark and try to understand why they did what they did. Criticism puts people on the defensive, wounds their pride and breeds resentment, and it almost never changes them. Story the author tells: The gunman Two Gun Crowley and Al Capone both saw themselves as decent men who had been wronged, and Crowley still blamed others as he went to the electric chair. Lincoln wrote a scathing letter to General Meade for letting Lee escape after Gettysburg, never sent it, and it was found among his papers after his death.

chapters.title: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
chapters.keys: Give honest, sincere appreciation. Notice what someone actually does well and tell them specifically, today, in plain words. People crave feeling important, and most go starved for real recognition. Story the author tells: Charles Schwab said he was paid a huge salary mainly for his skill in handling men, which came down to being hearty in approval and slow to find fault. A farm woman set a heap of hay before her men after years of cooking for them, saying they had never once said they noticed what she served.

chapters.title: He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way
chapters.keys: Arouse in the other person an eager want. Before you ask for something, work out what they want and show how your request gets it for them. People act on their own wants, not yours, so talk about theirs. Story the author tells: Emerson and his son pushed and pulled a calf that would not go into the barn, while their maid simply let it suck her finger and led it in. Andrew Carnegie bet he could get his silent nephews at college to write home by mentioning a check he did not enclose, and they promptly wrote to thank him.

chapters.title: Do This and You'll Be Welcome Anywhere
chapters.keys: Become genuinely interested in other people. Ask the people around you about their lives and remember what they tell you. You make more friends in two months by being interested in others than in two years of trying to get them interested in you. Story the author tells: The magician Howard Thurston told himself before each show that he loved his audience. Theodore Roosevelt phoned his valet's wife just to tell her a bird she had never seen was outside her window.

chapters.title: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
chapters.keys: Smile. Greet people with a warm, real smile, at the door, on the phone, at the desk. A smile tells people you are glad to see them, and if you do not feel like it, act cheerful until you do. Story the author tells: A New York stockbroker who rarely smiled at his wife began smiling at her, the doorman and everyone at work, and reported that his home life became happier and his business improved.

chapters.title: If You Don't Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
chapters.keys: Remember people's names. Learn the name, use it, and get it right. A person's name is to them the sweetest sound in any language. Story the author tells: Jim Farley, who never finished school, could call some fifty thousand people by first name and helped put Franklin Roosevelt in the White House. Andrew Carnegie as a boy got friends to feed his rabbits by naming the rabbits after them, and later used the same insight in business by naming things after the men he dealt with.

chapters.title: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
chapters.keys: Be a good listener and encourage others to talk about themselves. In your next conversation, ask questions and let the other person do the telling, with your full attention. People are far more interested in themselves than in you. Story the author tells: At a dinner Carnegie spent hours listening to a botanist talk about plants, barely speaking himself, and the botanist afterward called him a most interesting conversationalist.

chapters.title: How to Interest People
chapters.keys: Talk in terms of the other person's interests. Before meeting someone, find out what they care about and open with that. The royal road to a person's heart is to talk about what they treasure most. Story the author tells: Theodore Roosevelt read up the night before on whatever interested his next visitor. A Scout leader seeking a sponsor for a boy's trip asked a company president about a large check he had framed, never pressed his request, and the president paid more than was asked.

chapters.title: How to Make People Like You Instantly
chapters.keys: Make the other person feel important, and do it sincerely. Find something you honestly admire in the person in front of you, even a stranger, and say so. Everyone wants to feel important, and treating people that way is simply the golden rule. Story the author tells: Waiting in line at a post office, Carnegie told a bored clerk he admired his hair, and the clerk lit up; asked what he hoped to get from it, Carnegie said nothing at all.

chapters.title: You Can't Win an Argument
chapters.keys: The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it. When you feel a dispute coming, stop, look for what you agree on, and let the point go. Even if you win, the other person resents losing and is not convinced. Story the author tells: At a dinner Carnegie corrected a man who credited a quotation to the Bible, and his friend, a Shakespeare expert, sided with the man, then told Carnegie afterward there was no point embarrassing him. A truck salesman who used to argue with prospects started agreeing with their praise of rival trucks and began making sales.

chapters.title: A Sure Way of Making Enemies - and How to Avoid It
chapters.keys: Show respect for the other person's opinions and never tell them they are wrong. Say you may be mistaken and ask to look at the facts together. Telling someone flatly they are wrong attacks their pride and makes them dig in. Story the author tells: Benjamin Franklin, told as a young man that his blunt contradicting made him unbearable, stopped asserting things positively, spoke more tentatively, and found people far more willing to agree with him.

chapters.title: If You're Wrong, Admit It
chapters.keys: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically. Say it before the other person does, in stronger words than they would. It disarms them and they tend to become generous. Story the author tells: Carnegie let his small dog run unleashed in a park, and when a policeman caught him a second time, Carnegie admitted his fault before the officer could speak, and the officer eased off and let it pass.

chapters.title: A Drop of Honey
chapters.keys: Begin in a friendly way. Open a hard conversation, a complaint or a dispute, with warmth rather than anger. A drop of honey catches more flies than a gallon of gall, and people cannot be forced to agree with you. Story the author tells: John D. Rockefeller Jr. spoke as a friend to bitter, striking workers in Colorado and won them over. Aesop's sun warmed a man into taking off his coat where the wind's force failed.

chapters.title: The Secret of Socrates
chapters.keys: Get the other person saying yes, yes immediately. Start with points you both agree on and keep the conversation on common ground as long as you can. Once someone says no, pride makes them stick to it. Story the author tells: Socrates led opponents by questions they had to agree with until they accepted his conclusion. A bank teller won over a customer who refused to fill in a form by asking questions the man could only say yes to, and the customer filled it in.

chapters.title: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
chapters.keys: Let the other person do a great deal of the talking. When someone complains or you want their agreement, let them talk it all out without interrupting. They know more about their own problems than you do, and they will not listen while they still have things to say. Story the author tells: A salesman who had lost his voice to laryngitis could not make his pitch to a car company, the company's president talked for him, and he won the contract.

chapters.title: How to Get Cooperation
chapters.keys: Let the other person feel the idea is theirs. Instead of pushing your plan, ask for their input and let them shape it. People trust ideas they discover themselves far more than ones handed to them. Story the author tells: A sketch seller who had failed for years with one buyer brought unfinished sketches and asked how to finish them, and the buyer then bought them. Colonel House got his ideas adopted by Woodrow Wilson by letting Wilson think they were his own.

chapters.title: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
chapters.keys: Try honestly to see things from the other person's point of view. Before you correct or ask, picture why they are doing what they do and speak to that. People have reasons, and when you understand them you can work with them instead of against them. Story the author tells: Carnegie used to order boys away from fires they built under park trees and they resented it; later he spoke as one who understood the fun of a fire but showed them the danger, and they cooperated.

chapters.title: What Everybody Wants
chapters.keys: Be sympathetic with the other person's ideas and desires. When someone is upset, tell them you understand why they feel that way, and mean it. Sympathy calms anger more than any argument. Story the author tells: Carnegie misplaced Louisa May Alcott's home in a radio talk, got a furious letter from a listener, called her to say he understood her feelings, and she ended up apologizing and friendly.

chapters.title: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
chapters.keys: Appeal to nobler motives. When asking something of someone, speak to their sense of fairness and honor. People like to see themselves as honest and decent and will act up to it. Story the author tells: A landlord whose tenant wanted to break a lease told the man he believed him to be a man of his word, and the tenant stayed.

chapters.title: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don't You Do It?
chapters.keys: Dramatize your ideas. Show your point in a vivid, concrete way rather than only stating it. Plain facts are not enough; people respond to what they can see. Story the author tells: A Philadelphia newspaper accused of carrying too much advertising gathered one day's news and features into a book and sold it, showing how much reading it really gave.

chapters.title: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
chapters.keys: Throw down a challenge. When nothing else moves someone, give them a hard goal and a chance to prove themselves. People want to excel and to win. Story the author tells: Charles Schwab chalked the day shift's output on a mill floor, the night shift saw it and beat it, and production rose. Al Smith persuaded a reluctant man to run Sing Sing by framing it as a hard job for a big man, and he took it.

chapters.title: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
chapters.keys: Begin with praise and honest appreciation before you correct anyone. Open the conversation with something true you value about their work, then raise the problem. It is easier to hear the unpleasant after hearing something good. Story the author tells: Calvin Coolidge complimented his secretary's dress before telling her to watch her punctuation. A barber lathers a man before he shaves him.

chapters.title: How to Criticize - and Not Be Hated for It
chapters.keys: Call attention to people's mistakes indirectly. Instead of naming the fault outright, show the better way and let them see it. Direct criticism stirs resentment; indirect correction leaves dignity intact. Story the author tells: Charles Schwab found workers smoking under a No Smoking sign, gave each a cigar and asked them to smoke them outside. John Wanamaker, seeing a customer ignored while clerks chatted, served her himself and handed the purchase to the clerks to wrap.

chapters.title: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
chapters.keys: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person. Admit that you made the same kind of error before pointing out theirs. It is easier to hear criticism from someone who does not claim to be perfect. Story the author tells: Before correcting his young niece working as his secretary, Carnegie reminded himself and her of the far worse blunders he made at her age.

chapters.title: No One Likes to Take Orders
chapters.keys: Ask questions instead of giving direct orders. Say what do you think of this, or could we do it this way, rather than do this. It keeps pride intact, invites ideas, and people are more willing to carry out what they helped decide. Story the author tells: Owen D. Young was said never to give direct orders, only suggestions and questions.

chapters.title: Let the Other Person Save Face
chapters.keys: Let the other person save face. When you must correct, demote or overrule someone, do it privately and leave them their dignity. Hurting someone's dignity is a wrong, and they will not forget it. Story the author tells: General Electric moved the engineer Charles Steinmetz out of a department head job by giving him a new title as consulting engineer, and he was pleased.

chapters.title: How to Spur People On to Success
chapters.keys: Praise the slightest improvement and praise every improvement. Be hearty in approval and lavish in praise. Encouragement brings out ability that criticism kills. Story the author tells: An animal trainer praised and rewarded his dogs for each small improvement. A boy in Naples was told by a teacher he could not sing, but his mother praised his progress, and he became the great singer Caruso.

chapters.title: Give a Dog a Good Name
chapters.keys: Give the other person a fine reputation to live up to. Tell someone you trust them to do something well, assume they will, and say so. People will work hard not to disappoint a good opinion of them. Story the author tells: A woman hiring a maid who had been called sloppy told her she had heard she was neat and good, and the maid kept the house spotless.

chapters.title: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
chapters.keys: Use encouragement and make the fault seem easy to correct. Tell someone they have a knack for it and that the fix is easy. Tell them they are dumb and they stop trying. Story the author tells: Lowell Thomas told Carnegie, who thought he could never learn bridge, that it was easy and he had a natural gift, and Carnegie took it up.

chapters.title: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
chapters.keys: Make the other person happy about doing what you suggest. When you ask something, show them what they gain or how it honors them. People do willingly what makes them feel valued. Story the author tells: Woodrow Wilson sent Colonel House on a peace mission that William Jennings Bryan wanted, and House told Bryan he was too important to go, which pleased him.
